newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - French May jobless shows big rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - French May jobless shows big rise.

text.p: France's jobless total in May jumped by the biggest monthly amount in nearly four years, piling pressure on the new Socialist government to act swiftly on its election pledge to lower unemployment.
The number of people out of work climbed by 32,400 or 1.1 percent to 3,113,500, seasonally adjusted figures released by the employment ministry showed on Monday.
Private economists expressed surprise at the jump. Many had expected unemployment to be flat or little changed.

"It was a really big number and a really bad number. From a political standpoint, it's clearly a number that will put pressure on the government to take quick measures," said Eric Chaney, an economist at Morgan Stanley.

The Socialists swept to power on June 1, ousting the centre-right, on a promise to put fighting unemployment at the top of the political agenda and to qualify for Europe's planned new single currency without any more belt-tightening.
The unemployment rate, calculated according to International Labour Organisation (ILO) methods that strip out jobseekers who did any work, remained unchanged in May at 12.5 percent.
The ILO's method of calculating the jobless rate does not always move in tandem with the rate calculated using the French government's own method.

The rise in the raw jobless figures reversed three successive months of falls and was the biggest monthly increase since October 1993, the employment ministry said. Over one year, the number of jobseekers has risen by 2.3 percent.

Unemployment, which was a main contributor to the downfall of the previous conservative government, was higher among all age groups and both sexes. But joblessness among men between 25 and 40 showed the largest jump, climbing 1.5 percent.

Employment Minister Martine Aubry promised "total transparency" on unemployment which she called "French people's main worry". She said 1995 calculation changes had created a "climate of suspicion" about the reliability of the figures.
Under the previous method, the seasonally adjusted jobless total would have hit 3.5 million in May, the ministry said.

The figures brought calls from unions for fast action. "The government's priority must be the fight against unemployment. The priority must no longer be reduction of deficits," said Marc Blondel, head of the independent trade union Force Ouvriere.
Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has set a target of creating 700,000 jobs, half of them in the public sector, over the five-year life of the parliament.
But his scope for action has been curtailed by new estimates suggesting France's public deficit could sharply overshoot targets in the Maastricht treaty on monetary union.

The country's public deficit as a percentage of gross domestic product is headed for more than 3.4 or 3.5 percent of gross domestic product this year, far above the three percent Maastricht treaty goal, a government source said last week.
The Socialists' scant room to manoeuvre is unlikely to win sympathy from its Communist and left-wing coalition allies, already restive over what they see as backsliding by the Jospin administration.

"It (the unemployment figures) is very bad news," said Philippe Brossard, head of research at ABN Amro. "With such bad numbers, the fiscal policy which is moving to a more orthodox line, will be rejected even more vocally," he said.

A weekend decision by French carmaker Renault, in which the state holds a 46 percent stake, to go ahead with a controversial decision to shut a carplant in Belgium brought charges of broken promises from the Communists.
The Socialists promised during the campaign to push Renault to consider alternative to closing the Vilvoorde plant which employs 3,100.

Socialist Henri Emmanuelli, head of the National Assembly's finance commission, called Renault's move "very bad news for the Vilvoorde employees but also for all those who expect a different vision and action from the new coalition".
